name: The Kinzie house's fenced green
aka: the green 'inclosed between it and the river'

grade.why: Pictured: 2 of the pictures on the Images tab show it.

documented_range.note: The house's own range (kinzie_house_1812). THE KINZIE YEARS, BOTH ENDS INFERRED. It opens in the fall of 1804, when Currey has John Kinzie buy the house from Le Mai and arrive 'in the fall of that year' (currey_1912_story_of_old_fort_dearborn, ch. II); Moses and Kirkland give Le Mai 1796 where Currey gives 1797, and the Kinzies' arrival is put at 1803 elsewhere, so the opening is the later of the two readings and the house stands earlier than this phase says, under du Sable and Le Mai, in a form no picture shows. It covers 1 and 14 August 1812: Currey, 'The house escaped the general destruction at the time of the massacre'. It closes at the end of 1833: Currey says it 'was finally demolished in the early thirties', the 1857 engraving shows it about 1833, and data/exclusions.json kinzie_house rules it unoccupied and 'dilapidated beyond repair' from 1832 and gone by 1835, so it stands in no 1835 view.

placement.position_note: Wau-Bun: 'A broad green space was inclosed between it and the river'. Its north side runs along the piazza and its south side along the bank top, where the 1812 ground's level 1.5 m stands; its width, a house-length and a half either side of the door, is read off the 1832 and 1833 pictures, which carry the fence well east of the house to take in the poplars. The corners are this record's own (docs/LIBERTIES.md L-kinzie-house-1812-2497).
placement.symbolic_location: Before the Kinzie house, from just off its piazza (local N +333.5) to the top of the e1830_natural north bank (N +318), E +1132.5 to E +1171.5, centred on the house's door. The origin is the fence's south-west corner.

footprint.note: The fence line. Thirty-nine metres along the river by fifteen and a half to the bank.

wall_kind.note: Both engravings draw a fence of close-set pickets round the green, not rails.

construction.note: Split pales, the archetype's light-post kind.

picket_height_m.note: About rail-high: both engravings draw the pickets level with the piazza's rail.

picket_width_m.note: Unattested. A sawn or split paling.

picket_spacing_m.note: Unattested. Close set, as both engravings hatch them.

gate_sides.note: Unattested. A gate before the door, so the piazza opens onto the green.

gate_width_m.note: Unattested. A walk's width, and the narrowest gate the archetype builds.

function.note: Wau-Bun ch. XVII: 'A broad green space was inclosed between it and the river, and shaded by a row of Lombardy poplars.' The grass inside is the 1812 ground's own cover; only the fence is built.

land_owner.value: The ground was entered by Robert A Kenzie, 7 May 1831
land_owner.note: KINZIE'S ADDITION. The north fraction of section 10 is the section north of the river, which is why the register prints 102.29 acres and not a quarter's 160. It is resolved as the section's own grid box clipped to the committed north bank of the main stem (`e1834_harbor_cut/shoreline.geojson`), so no boundary here is authored. The two rows the register carries for it — one plain, one with the school-section marker — are the same entry printed twice. THE REGISTER SPELLS THE PURCHASER MORE THAN ONE WAY for this same tract — Robert A Kenzie; Robert A Kinzie — and the spellings are carried rather than merged, which is the land_sales crosswalk's standing rule: tract agreement is where two spellings MIGHT be one man and is never proof that they are. THE MARGIN IS ONLY 16 m, which is inside the working horizontal uncertainty of the georeference (about 20 m) doubled, so the grade drops a tier: the tract is right if the constructed line is, and nothing here proves the line to better than that. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

citations.citation: "The Kinzie House" — wood engraving, in The Chicago Magazine: The West As It Is, vol. 1 no. 1 (Chicago, March 1857); reprinted by A. T. Andreas, History of Chicago vol. 1 (1884), where it is captioned as the old Kinzie house about 1833.
what_it_supplies: the house long and low under a gable roof running along the river, with two stacks through the ridge, about 0.45 and 0.93 of it from the west gable
the piazza across the whole front on slender posts, under its own flatter roof below the main eave, with a railing between the posts
a door at the middle of the front with windows either side
the picket fence enclosing a green before the piazza, toward the water
four columnar Lombardy poplars in a row along the green's river-side fence, from opposite the house's east half to beyond its east end
a big broad-crowned tree behind the house
what_it_does_not_supply: the house in 1812: it shows it about twenty years later

citations.citation: Currey, J. Seymour. The Story of Old Fort Dearborn. Chicago: A. C. McClurg & Co., 1912.
what_it_supplies: the house's builder, Jean Baptiste Point de Saible, 'a native of San Domingo and a negro', and that he built it 'some time before 1779' near the present foot of Pine Street
its sale in 1797 to Le Mai, and Le Mai's sale to John Kinzie in 1804, Kinzie arriving 'in the fall of that year'
Kinzie's work on it: 'he repaired it, added a veranda, and planted four Lombardy poplars at the foot of the slope on which the house stood'
its orientation: 'The house faced toward the south, having the river directly in front and the lake a short distance to the east'
that it 'escaped the general destruction at the time of the massacre' and 'was finally demolished in the early thirties'
Ouilmette's cabin 'close in the rear of the Kinzie house' and Pettell's 'small cabin near the Kinzie house'

the lake shore south of the river mouth before 1812, in the same chapter: 'mostly devoid of trees, a scanty growth of cottonwoods and pines, however, maintaining a precarious existence among the sand-dunes', the low sand-hills 'the predominant feature of the landscape' a mile or two south of the mouth (used by T-2768 for the pines on the south sand hills)
what_it_does_not_supply: any dimension of the house, the piazza or the green
the number of the house's rooms, windows or chimneys
a date for the veranda or the poplars more exact than 'after the house came into the possession of John Kinzie'
the Sarony lithograph itself: the Gutenberg file carries only its caption, so the plate is not read here

citations.citation: Illinois State Archives, Illinois Public Domain Land Tract Sales Database (Springfield: Office of the Secretary of State).
Kinzie, Juliette A. M. Wau-Bun: The 'Early Day' in the North-West. New York: Derby & Jackson, 1856.
"KINZIE MANSION AND FORT DEARBORN." — wood engraving, in Benson J. Lossing, The Pictorial Field-Book of the War of 1812 (New York: Harper & Brothers, 1869).
what_it_supplies: a long, low, single-storey house on the north bank, its ridge parallel to the river, gables at its ends
a piazza across its front on square posts, under a flatter roof hung below the main eave
two stacks rising through the ridge, one about 0.4 of it from the west gable and one near the west gable
a low picket fence before the house enclosing a green to the water, and a row of tall columnar poplars beside it
a large broad-crowned tree behind the house at the west end
the first fort's picket line and blockhouses across the river, which is what the plate claims to date
what_it_does_not_supply: any dimension or position: it is a tier-5 retrospective view, form only
an eyewitness: Lossing drew it more than fifty years after the fort burned, and his sources for it are not stated on the plate

research_note: THE GREEN BEFORE THE KINZIE HOUSE (T-2497). Only the paling is built; the poplars that shade it and the two cottonwoods behind the house are data/flora/plantings/kinzie_house_1812_trees.json.
